questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 3 days of nausea, anorexia, malaise, and vomiting. On examination her sclerae are icteric, her skin is jaundiced, and the right upper quadrant is tender. Which underlying process best explains her scleral icterus and jaundice?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accelerated splenic destruction of red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deposition of iron in the skin and sclerae

explanation.summary: Jaundice in hepatitis reflects hepatocellular injury impairing bilirubin handling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inflamed, injured hepatocytes cannot conjugate and excrete bilirubin normally, so it accumulates in serum and deposits in the skin, sclerae, and mucous membranes as jaundice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin synthesis falls (not rises) in liver disease, and low albumin does not cause jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin but is not the mechanism in viral hepatitis, where the defect is hepatocellular.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cystic duct obstruction causes biliary colic/cholecystitis, not the diffuse hepatocellular picture with systemic viral symptoms described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron deposition (hemochromatosis) causes bronze skin over years, not acute icterus with a 3-day viral prodrome.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient with acute hepatitis is noted to have dark urine and pale, clay-colored stools. Which finding best explains this combination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased gut excretion of conjugated bilirubin, spilling into urine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased production of unconjugated bilirubin from hemolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired urobilinogen reabsorption in the terminal ileum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated serum ammonia from impaired hepatic detoxification

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced hepatic synthesis of the vitamin K–dependent clotting factors

explanation.summary: Dark urine plus pale stools reflects conjugated bilirubin diverted from gut to urine.
explanation.whyCorrect: When hepatocellular injury reduces excretion of conjugated bilirubin into the biliary tract, less pigment reaches the gut (pale stools) while water-soluble conjugated bilirubin spills into the blood and is filtered into urine (dark urine, bilirubinuria on dipstick).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Unconjugated bilirubin is not water soluble and does not appear in urine, so hemolysis does not produce bilirubinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urobilinogen handling is not the primary driver of the dark-urine/pale-stool pattern; reduced conjugated bilirubin excretion is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated ammonia contributes to encephalopathy, not to urine or stool color.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Impaired clotting-factor synthesis prolongs the PT/INR but does not change urine or stool color.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A hepatology attending reminds students that although the panel is called “liver function tests,” several components actually measure hepatocyte injury rather than function. Which of the following is a true test of hepatic synthetic function?

explanation.summary: Albumin, PT, and bilirubin reflect function; transaminases and ALP reflect injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Albumin is synthesized by hepatocytes, so its level (along with prothrombin time and bilirubin) reflects true liver function. Transaminases and cholestatic enzymes are released from or induced by injured cells and mark injury, not function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ALT is released from damaged hepatocytes and is a marker of injury, not synthetic function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AST likewise reflects hepatocellular injury and is also found in muscle and other tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ALP is a cholestatic injury/obstruction marker, not a measure of synthetic function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GGT is a cholestatic marker used to confirm the hepatic origin of an elevated ALP, not a function test.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient with severe acute hepatitis develops confusion and asterixis. Laboratory studies show a prolonged prothrombin time and elevated serum ammonia. These abnormalities are best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute obstruction of the common bile duct

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic islet cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased renal excretion of clotting factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bacterial overgrowth of the small intestine

explanation.summary: Coagulopathy plus hyperammonemia signals failing hepatic synthetic/detox capacity.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prolonged PT/INR reflects failed synthesis of clotting factors, and elevated ammonia reflects impaired hepatic detoxification; together they indicate the liver's synthetic and detoxifying functions are failing, as in acute (fulminant) liver failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Biliary obstruction causes cholestasis and jaundice but does not by itself cause hyperammonemia and coagulopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Islet-cell destruction causes diabetes, unrelated to PT prolongation or ammonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clotting factors are proteins made by the liver, not lost through the kidney; the defect is decreased synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small-bowel bacterial overgrowth causes malabsorption, not acute coagulopathy with encephalopathy.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops fever, malaise, anorexia, and jaundice 3 weeks after returning from a backpacking trip through rural regions with poor sanitation, where he drank untreated water. He does not use injection drugs. Which virus is the most likely cause, and what is its expected course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatitis B virus; frequently progresses to chronic infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatitis C virus; up to 85% become chronically infected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatitis A virus; acute, self-limited, no chronicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatitis D virus; requires concurrent hepatitis B infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus; latent infection with periodic reactivation

explanation.summary: Fecal–oral exposure with a short prodrome points to HAV, an acute self-limited illness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis A is acquired by the fecal–oral route (contaminated food/water, poor sanitation), has a 2–6 week incubation, and causes an acute, self-limited infection that does not become chronic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HBV is bloodborne/sexual/perinatal, not typically from contaminated water, and this exposure history fits fecal–oral transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HCV is parenteral and this man denies injection drug use or other bloodborne risk; the travel/water history fits HAV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HDV can only infect with HBV present, and nothing here indicates HBV coinfection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CMV hepatitis occurs mainly in immunocompromised or perinatal settings, not after ingesting contaminated water in a healthy traveler.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: The risk that acute hepatitis B becomes a chronic infection depends strongly on the age at which infection is acquired. Approximately what proportion of infants infected perinatally progress to chronic HBV infection?

explanation.summary: Perinatal HBV becomes chronic in up to ~90% of infants; adult infection rarely does.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronicity risk for HBV is inversely related to age at infection: up to ~90% of infants infected perinatally become chronically infected, versus only about 5–10% of adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Less than 1% understates the very high perinatal chronicity risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 5–10% is the chronicity rate for adult-acquired HBV, not perinatal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 25% does not match the established perinatal figure of roughly 90%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 50% still understates perinatal chronicity, which approaches 90%.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A hepatitis virus is described as an enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus whose RNA-dependent RNA polymerase lacks proofreading activity, producing rapid antigenic variation of its envelope proteins. This feature best explains which clinical consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An exclusively fecal–oral route of transmission

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dependence on a coinfecting helper virus for replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of ground-glass hepatocytes on biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: High rate of chronic infection from immune evasion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reliably protective immunity after natural infection

explanation.summary: This describes HCV: an error-prone polymerase drives antigenic variation and chronicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The virus is hepatitis C (Flavivirus). Its error-prone polymerase generates constant envelope-protein variation, allowing immune evasion and a high rate (up to ~85%) of progression to chronic infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HCV is bloodborne (parenteral), not fecal–oral; fecal–oral applies to HAV and HEV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Requiring a helper virus describes HDV, which needs HBV, not HCV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ground-glass hepatocytes are characteristic of HBV, not HCV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HCV antibodies do NOT confer protective immunity; reinfection can occur, unlike after HBV immunity.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis B is found to have a superimposed second hepatitis virus, and his disease progresses unexpectedly rapidly toward liver failure. This second virus can only replicate in the presence of hepatitis B. Which virus is responsible?

explanation.summary: A defective virus needing HBsAg to replicate, causing severe superinfection, is HDV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis D is a defective, circular RNA virus (Deltavirus) that requires hepatitis B for replication. Superinfection of a chronic HBV carrier increases the risk of severe disease and accelerated progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HAV is an independent, acute, self-limited virus that does not depend on HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HCV replicates independently and does not require HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HEV replicates independently and does not require HBV; it is notable for severity in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: EBV causes mononucleosis and can involve the liver but does not require HBV to replicate.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A liver biopsy from a patient with chronic viral hepatitis shows hepatocytes with a pale, finely granular (“ground-glass”) cytoplasm. This finding results from accumulation of which substance, and it indicates infection with which virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the ER; HBV

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fat vacuoles displacing the nucleus; steatotic liver disease

explanation.summary: Ground-glass hepatocytes come from HBsAg buildup in the ER and indicate HBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ground-glass hepatocytes have pale, granular cytoplasm caused by accumulation of HBsAg in the endoplasmic reticulum and are characteristic of chronic hepatitis B infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mallory-Denk bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of alcoholic (and steatotic) liver injury, not the ground-glass pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Owl's-eye inclusions are intranuclear and characteristic of CMV, not the cytoplasmic ground-glass change of HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron accumulation is seen in hemochromatosis and is demonstrated with a Prussian blue stain, not as ground-glass cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fat vacuoles indicate steatosis, a different morphologic change from ground-glass hepatocytes.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: An immunocompromised transplant recipient develops hepatitis. Liver biopsy shows enlarged cells with large intranuclear “owl's-eye” inclusions. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions in an immunocompromised host indicate CMV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytomegalovirus produces characteristic large “owl's-eye” intranuclear inclusions and causes hepatitis as part of systemic infection, especially in immunocompromised patients or perinatal infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HBV produces cytoplasmic ground-glass hepatocytes, not owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Entamoeba causes a solitary hepatic abscess (anchovy-paste), not owl's-eye inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HAV causes acute self-limited hepatitis without distinctive inclusion bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fasciola is a liver fluke that infects the biliary tree; it does not produce owl's-eye inclusions.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A previously healthy person develops fulminant acute liver failure. Because this cause is highly fatal without treatment yet responds to early empiric antiviral therapy, it is considered a “must not miss” diagnosis even though it rarely causes hepatitis. Which pathogen–treatment pair is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatitis A virus — supportive care only

explanation.summary: HSV hepatitis is rare but often fatal; empiric acyclovir can be lifesaving.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV rarely causes hepatitis, but when it does it frequently causes highly fatal fulminant liver failure. It is a high-stakes “must not miss” diagnosis, and early empiric acyclovir—often given before confirmatory PCR—can be lifesaving.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HAV is self-limited and managed supportively; it is not the fulminant “must not miss” diagnosis requiring empiric antivirals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV causes chronic disease treated electively with DAAs, not fulminant failure needing emergent empiric therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: EBV hepatitis is usually self-limited; steroids are reserved for airway obstruction, not to prevent fulminant liver failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HEV is usually self-limited (severe mainly in pregnancy); it is not the classic acyclovir-responsive fulminant hepatitis.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A pregnant woman in her third trimester develops acute hepatitis after traveling to a region with poor sanitation. Which hepatitis virus is most associated with an increased risk of acute liver failure in pregnancy?

explanation.summary: HEV, a fecal–oral virus, carries a high risk of acute liver failure in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis E is transmitted fecal–orally and is usually acute and self-limited, but it is specifically associated with a markedly increased risk of acute (fulminant) liver failure in pregnant women.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HAV is fecal–oral and usually mild; it lacks the specific pregnancy-associated fulminant risk of HEV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HBV is bloodborne and does not have the distinctive pregnancy-related fulminant course of HEV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HCV is bloodborne and tends to be chronic; it is not the classic pregnancy-associated fulminant hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HDV requires HBV and is not the fecal–oral pregnancy-associated virus; the traveler's exposure fits HEV.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient with suspected acute hepatitis A infection is tested. Which single serologic marker best confirms acute HAV infection?

explanation.summary: Anti-HAV IgM is the earliest marker and confirms acute HAV infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-HAV IgM is the earliest detectable serologic marker and indicates acute HAV infection. Anti-HAV IgG appears later and signifies past infection or vaccination with long-term immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-HAV IgG indicates past infection or immunity, not acute infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HAV RNA appears early but is not the routine clinical test; antibody testing is the first-line approach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-HBc IgM is a marker of acute hepatitis B, not hepatitis A.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-HCV IgG is a marker of hepatitis C exposure, unrelated to HAV.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient's hepatitis B panel returns during a specific phase of recovery: HBsAg is negative, anti-HBs is negative, and anti-HBc IgM is positive. Which interpretation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic active hepatitis B with high infectivity

choices.label: B
choices.text: The "window period," with anti-HBc IgM as the only marker

choices.label: C
choices.text: Successful prior vaccination against hepatitis B

choices.label: D
choices.text: Distant resolved infection with lifelong immunity

choices.label: E
choices.text: A false-positive result that requires no additional testing

explanation.summary: HBsAg–, anti-HBs–, anti-HBc IgM+ defines the HBV window period.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the window period, HBsAg has become undetectable but anti-HBs has not yet appeared; anti-HBc IgM may be the only positive marker, so testing for it is essential to catch infection during this gap.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic active HBV shows persistent HBsAg (and often HBeAg/HBV DNA), not a negative HBsAg.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vaccination produces isolated anti-HBs positivity with negative anti-HBc, the opposite pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resolved infection shows anti-HBs positive and anti-HBc IgG positive; here anti-HBs is negative and the core antibody is IgM.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pattern is a classic window period, not a spurious result to ignore.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A hepatitis B panel shows HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, and HBeAg positive, with elevated HBV DNA, persisting beyond 6 months. What does the HBeAg finding indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resolution of infection and developing immunity

choices.label: B
choices.text: A protective response to hepatitis B vaccination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recent coinfection with hepatitis D virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute infection within the past two weeks

explanation.summary: HBeAg marks high HBV replication and infectivity in active chronic infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: HBeAg reflects high viral replication and infectivity. Its presence with persistent HBsAg and HBV DNA beyond 6 months indicates active chronic hepatitis B; in inactive chronic disease, HBeAg is absent and anti-HBe is present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resolution/immunity is marked by loss of HBsAg and appearance of anti-HBs, not by HBeAg positivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vaccination yields isolated anti-HBs; it does not produce HBeAg.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HDV coinfection is detected with anti-HDV and HDV RNA, not by HBeAg.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Persistence beyond 6 months indicates chronic, not recent acute, infection.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient's anti-HCV IgG antibody test is positive. Which test is required next to determine whether the patient has an active hepatitis C infection?

explanation.summary: A positive anti-HCV IgG requires HCV RNA to confirm active infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-HCV IgG indicates exposure but does not distinguish active from resolved infection. HCV RNA (PCR) is the earliest and most specific marker of active infection and is used to confirm whether the virus is still present.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Repeating the antibody adds nothing, because anti-HCV IgG persists after both resolved and treated infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-HCV IgM is not the standard confirmatory test; HCV RNA is used to confirm active infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HBsAg tests for hepatitis B, not for active hepatitis C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Biopsy assesses disease severity, not whether active HCV infection is present; RNA testing answers that.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: For which patients is testing for hepatitis D virus specifically recommended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All patients with a positive anti-HAV IgG

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients with isolated anti-HBs from vaccination

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients with a positive Monospot test

explanation.summary: HDV testing is indicated in HBsAg-positive patients, since HDV requires HBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because HDV can only replicate in the presence of hepatitis B, testing (anti-HDV, then HDV RNA to confirm active infection) is recommended in HBsAg-positive patients, especially those with unexpectedly severe or rapidly progressive disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-HAV IgG reflects hepatitis A immunity and gives no indication for HDV testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isolated anti-HBs from vaccination means no HBV infection, so HDV—which needs HBV—cannot occur.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated transaminases alone are nonspecific and are not the criterion; HBsAg positivity is.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive Monospot indicates EBV (heterophile antibodies), unrelated to HDV testing.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A medical student asks which forms of viral hepatitis can currently be prevented with an effective vaccine in routine use. Which pair is correct?

explanation.summary: Only HAV and HBV have widely used effective vaccines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Effective, routinely used vaccines exist for hepatitis A and hepatitis B. There is no widely available vaccine for HCV or CMV, and HDV is prevented indirectly through HBV vaccination (no independent HDV vaccine).

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no vaccine for hepatitis C, so this pair is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis C has no vaccine; only the HAV half of this pair is correct.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither HCV nor an independent HDV vaccine exists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no CMV vaccine in routine use; HBV is the only correct member here.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis C develops palpable purpura, arthralgias, and glomerulonephritis. Serum contains immunoglobulins that precipitate in the cold. Which extrahepatic manifestation of HCV does this represent?

explanation.summary: Cold-precipitating immunoglobulins with vasculitis and GN indicate HCV mixed cryoglobulinemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic hepatitis C is classically associated with mixed cryoglobulinemia—cold-precipitating immune complexes causing small-vessel vasculitis (palpable purpura, arthralgias) and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Polyarteritis nodosa is the vasculitis classically linked to hepatitis B, not HCV cryoglobulinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membranous nephropathy is the HBV-associated glomerular lesion; HCV is linked to membranoproliferative GN with cryoglobulins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serum sickness–like syndrome is a hepatitis B–associated presentation, not the cryoglobulinemic vasculitis of HCV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Porphyria cutanea tarda is an HCV-associated skin finding but does not explain cold-precipitating immunoglobulins with vasculitis and glomerulonephritis.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis B develops a small- and medium-vessel vasculitis with abdominal pain, hypertension, and mononeuritis multiplex, along with a membranous glomerular lesion. Which pair of extrahepatic manifestations is most characteristic of hepatitis B?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mixed cryoglobulinemia and porphyria cutanea tarda

explanation.summary: HBV is classically associated with polyarteritis nodosa and membranous nephropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatitis B is characteristically linked to polyarteritis nodosa (a small/medium-vessel vasculitis) and membranous nephropathy, along with serum sickness–like syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mixed cryoglobulinemia and porphyria cutanea tarda are hepatitis C–associated, not HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membranoproliferative GN and lichen planus are hepatitis C–associated manifestations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 2 diabetes and thyroiditis are among hepatitis C–associated conditions, not the classic HBV pair.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sicca syndrome and caries relate to Sjögren syndrome, not to hepatitis B.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with fatigue, jaundice, and right upper quadrant discomfort. She denies alcohol and injection drug use. ALT and AST are elevated but viral hepatitis serologies are all negative. Further testing shows elevated serum IgG with positive ANA and anti–smooth muscle antibodies, and liver biopsy shows portal and periportal inflammation with prominent plasma cell infiltrates. What is the most appropriate treatment?

explanation.summary: Negative viral serologies with ANA/ASMA, high IgG, and plasma cells indicate autoimmune hepatitis, treated with immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: The picture—negative viral serologies, elevated IgG, positive ANA and ASMA, and plasma cell–rich portal inflammation—is autoimmune hepatitis. First-line therapy is immunosuppression with prednisone plus the steroid-sparing agent azathioprine, which improves long-term survival.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Entecavir treats chronic hepatitis B, but HBV serologies are negative here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Supportive care alone suits self-limited acute viral hepatitis (e.g., HAV), not progressive autoimmune hepatitis, which requires immunosuppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Direct-acting antivirals treat hepatitis C; HCV serologies are negative in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribavirin plus interferon is an older hepatitis C regimen, not a treatment for autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.topicName: Viral Hepatitis: Presentation, Diagnosis, and Autoimmune Comparison
questions.stem: Which set of laboratory and histologic findings best distinguishes autoimmune hepatitis from acute viral hepatitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated IgG, positive ANA/ASMA, plasma-cell–rich inflammation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Positive HBsAg with ground-glass hepatocytes on biopsy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Positive anti-HAV IgM with spotty hepatocyte necrosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive HCV RNA with lymphocytic portal inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Owl's-eye intranuclear inclusions with a systemic viral prodrome

explanation.summary: Autoimmune hepatitis: high IgG, ANA/ASMA, and plasma cell infiltrates with negative viral markers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoimmune hepatitis is distinguished by elevated serum IgG, positive ANA and anti–smooth muscle antibodies, and biopsy showing portal/periportal inflammation with a plasma cell–predominant infiltrate, in the setting of negative viral serologies.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Positive HBsAg with ground-glass hepatocytes indicates hepatitis B, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-HAV IgM indicates acute hepatitis A, a viral cause, not autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive HCV RNA indicates hepatitis C infection, not autoimmune hepatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Owl's-eye inclusions indicate CMV infection, a viral cause.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man presents with several weeks of intermittent fever and dull right upper quadrant pain. Six months ago he spent two weeks doing mission work in rural central Africa. Temperature is 100.1 F. Labs show leukocytosis and mildly elevated aminotransferases. CT reveals a single, well-defined cyst in the right hepatic lobe; the gallbladder is normal. Which organism is the most likely cause of his condition?

explanation.summary: A solitary right-lobe hepatic abscess in a traveler returning from an endemic region points to amebic liver abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: Entamoeba histolytica causes solitary right-lobe abscesses via portal spread and is the classic cause of hepatic abscess linked to travel in endemic tropical/subtropical regions with poor sanitation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: E coli causes pyogenic abscess, typically from ascending cholangitis, and produces multiple lesions rather than a single traveler-associated cyst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Klebsiella pyogenic abscess is not tied to a tropical travel history and is usually associated with diabetes, not a single well-defined post-travel cyst.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Candida causes multiple microabscesses in immunocompromised patients, not a solitary lesion in an otherwise healthy traveler.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clonorchis infects the biliary tree from raw freshwater fish and causes cholangitis/cholangiocarcinoma risk, not a solitary hepatic cyst after African travel.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a recent episode of ascending cholangitis presents with fever and right upper quadrant pain. CT shows multiple septated fluid collections in the liver. Blood cultures grow a gram-negative rod. In the United States, which organism is the single most common cause of this type of abscess?

explanation.summary: Pyogenic liver abscess from ascending cholangitis is most commonly caused by E coli in the US.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ascending cholangitis due to E coli is the most common cause of pyogenic (bacterial) liver abscess in the United States, consistent with multiple lesions and gram-negative bacteremia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: S aureus abscesses arise from hematogenous seeding (e.g., endocarditis) but are not the most common US cause and are gram-positive cocci, not the gram-negative rod described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: E histolytica is the most common cause outside the US and yields solitary lesions, not multiple septated collections from cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Candida causes fungal abscesses in immunocompromised hosts, not the leading cause after cholangitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacteroides is a common anaerobic co-pathogen in polymicrobial pyogenic abscess but is not the single most common isolate and is not the gram-negative rod grown here.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is being evaluated for suspected hepatic abscess. Which single laboratory abnormality is the most characteristic finding in this condition?

explanation.summary: Alkaline phosphatase is the most characteristic lab abnormality in hepatic abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alkaline phosphatase rises due to inflammation and obstruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts and ductules, making it the most characteristic laboratory finding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilirubin may be normal or only mildly elevated and is not the most characteristic finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thrombocytopenia is nonspecific and not a hallmark of hepatic abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypoglycemia is not a characteristic feature of hepatic abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated lipase indicates pancreatic injury, not hepatic abscess.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old diabetic man with fever and right upper quadrant pain has CT showing two multiloculated hepatic fluid collections. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are started. What is the most appropriate additional intervention?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Observation with repeat imaging in 3 months

explanation.summary: Pyogenic liver abscess is managed with broad-spectrum antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Multiloculated bacterial (pyogenic) abscesses typically require CT-guided percutaneous drainage in addition to antibiotics, and drained fluid is cultured to guide targeted therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metronidazole/paromomycin treats amebic abscess, not a pyogenic abscess in a diabetic with multiloculated bacterial collections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Triclabendazole treats fascioliasis, not a bacterial abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An echinocandin treats fungal (Candida) abscess in immunocompromised patients, not this bacterial abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Watchful observation is inappropriate for a symptomatic multiloculated pyogenic abscess that needs drainage.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old immigrant from South Asia is diagnosed with an amebic liver abscess. Which sequential regimen is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Amebic abscess requires a tissue amebicide followed by a luminal amebicide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metronidazole (tissue amebicide) kills invasive trophozoites, and paromomycin (luminal amebicide) is given afterward to eradicate residual intestinal cysts and prevent relapse or transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ceftriaxone is an antibacterial agent with no activity against E histolytica.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Triclabendazole treats fascioliasis, not luminal amebic cysts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Praziquantel and albendazole are antihelminthics for flukes and other worms, not amebiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic without reliable antiamebic activity and does not clear luminal cysts.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man from a rural farming community in the Andes reports eating raw watercress salads. He develops right upper quadrant pain, fever, and marked eosinophilia. Imaging suggests migratory tracks in the liver. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: Fascioliasis is acquired by eating cyst-bearing aquatic plants such as watercress and causes eosinophilia with hepatic migration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fasciola hepatica is transmitted by ingesting metacercariae on aquatic plants (watercress); larvae penetrate the intestine and migrate through the liver, producing eosinophilia and hepatic tracks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonorchis is acquired from raw freshwater fish, not aquatic plants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opisthorchis is also acquired from raw/undercooked fish, not watercress.
whyWrongByChoice.D: E histolytica causes a solitary abscess from portal spread, not plant-borne larval migration with eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Echinococcus causes a hydatid cyst acquired from dog tapeworm eggs, not from watercress, and typically without prominent migratory eosinophilic hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man who regularly eats raw freshwater fish in Southeast Asia is found to have chronic biliary inflammation. His physician counsels him that this parasitic infection increases his lifetime risk of which malignancy?

explanation.summary: Clonorchis sinensis infection is a risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic infection with the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis (from raw freshwater fish) causes chronic biliary inflammation and is an established risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma, a bile duct malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma is linked to hepatitis B/C and cirrhosis, not liver fluke biliary infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gallbladder carcinoma is associated with gallstones and porcelain gallbladder, not Clonorchis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pancreatic cancer is not the malignancy classically linked to liver flukes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastric cancer is associated with H pylori and dietary factors, not Clonorchis.

questions.stem: During percutaneous aspiration of a solitary right-lobe hepatic abscess in a returning traveler, the physician obtains homogeneous, reddish-brown liquefied material described as anchovy paste. This appearance results from which process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial gas production within the cavity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fungal hyphae mixed with necrotic tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cholesterol-rich bile leaking into the abscess

choices.label: D
choices.text: Layered calcification of the abscess wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parasitic proteolysis of hepatocytes and blood

explanation.summary: Anchovy paste aspirate is characteristic of amebic abscess and reflects proteolytic tissue digestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reddish-brown anchovy paste material is produced by Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite proteases digesting hepatocytes and blood, liquefying the necrotic core.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gas production reflects gas-forming bacteria, not the anchovy paste appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fungal abscesses form microabscesses and are not described as anchovy paste.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bile leakage does not produce the classic reddish-brown proteolytic aspirate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wall calcification is a feature of chronic/hydatid disease, not the liquefied amebic aspirate.

questions.stem: A researcher is describing why portal vein-borne infections such as amebic abscess preferentially involve one region of the liver. Which lobe is most commonly affected and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Left lobe, because it receives most inferior mesenteric flow

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caudate lobe, because it drains directly to the vena cava

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quadrate lobe, because of its central biliary location

choices.label: D
choices.text: Left lobe, because it is closest to the hepatic artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Right lobe, because it contains two thirds of liver mass

explanation.summary: The right hepatic lobe is preferentially involved because it holds most of the liver mass and receives streaming portal flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The right lobe contains roughly two thirds of total liver mass and receives disproportionate superior mesenteric venous streaming, so portal-borne organisms lodge there most often.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The left lobe is smaller and less commonly involved by portal-borne disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The caudate lobe has unique venous drainage but is not the preferential site for portal-borne abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The quadrate lobe is not the region preferentially seeded by portal flow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Proximity to the hepatic artery does not explain the right-lobe predominance of portal-borne infection.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old traveler with suspected amebic liver abscess undergoes workup. Which test provides the greatest sensitivity and specificity for confirming Entamoeba histolytica?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Routine stool ova and parasite microscopy

explanation.summary: E histolytica antigen/serologic testing is more accurate than stool microscopy for amebic abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: An E histolytica antigen test (with supportive serology) has higher sensitivity and specificity than routine ova and parasite microscopy, which cannot reliably distinguish E histolytica from nonpathogenic species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Routine stool O&P is nonspecific and often negative in extraintestinal amebic abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blood cultures are useful for pyogenic abscess but do not detect E histolytica.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alkaline phosphatase is a nonspecific marker of hepatic abscess, not a confirmatory test for the organism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peripheral smear does not identify E histolytica; the parasite is not a blood-stage organism detected this way.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with a diagnosed amebic liver abscess is treated with metronidazole and clinically improves. Why must a luminal agent such as paromomycin be added?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Metronidazole cannot penetrate liver abscess tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paromomycin provides better analgesia for RUQ pain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metronidazole does not reliably clear intestinal cysts

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paromomycin drains the abscess cavity chemically

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metronidazole is ineffective against invasive trophozoites

explanation.summary: A luminal amebicide is needed because metronidazole does not eradicate intestinal cysts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metronidazole kills tissue-invading trophozoites but does not reliably clear luminal cysts, so paromomycin is added to eliminate residual intestinal cysts and prevent relapse and transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metronidazole penetrates liver tissue well; that is precisely why it treats the abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Paromomycin is not an analgesic and is not added for pain control.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paromomycin acts within the intestinal lumen and does not chemically drain the abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metronidazole is effective against invasive trophozoites; its limitation is luminal cyst clearance.

questions.stem: A neutropenic 29-year-old woman recovering from induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia has persistent fever despite broad-spectrum antibiotics. CT shows multiple small target-like microabscesses scattered throughout the liver and spleen. Which treatment is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Multiple hepatosplenic microabscesses in a neutropenic patient indicate hepatosplenic candidiasis, treated with an antifungal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fungal (Candida) hepatic abscesses occur in immunocompromised patients, present as multiple microabscesses with fever refractory to antibiotics, and are treated with an echinocandin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Metronidazole/paromomycin treats amebiasis, not Candida.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Triclabendazole treats fascioliasis, not fungal microabscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Praziquantel treats liver flukes, not Candida.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Drainage alone does not address disseminated fungal microabscesses, which require systemic antifungal therapy.

questions.stem: A parasitologist is reviewing the Fasciola hepatica life cycle. Which stage is directly infectious to humans?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adult worm in the bile duct

explanation.summary: Humans are infected by ingesting metacercariae encysted on aquatic plants.
explanation.whyCorrect: The metacercaria is the infectious stage; it encysts on aquatic plants (or in fish for other flukes) and, once ingested, excysts in the small intestine and migrates to the liver.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eggs are shed in feces to continue the cycle in water and are not infectious to humans by ingestion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Miracidia infect the snail intermediate host, not humans.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adult worms reside in the biliary tree of an already-infected host and are not the transmissible stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cercariae are released from snails and encyst as metacercariae; the cercaria itself is not the human-infective form for Fasciola.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with clonorchiasis after eating raw freshwater fish. Which agent is the preferred treatment?

explanation.summary: Praziquantel is the preferred treatment for clonorchiasis and opisthorchiasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Praziquantel is preferred for clonorchiasis and opisthorchiasis; it causes rapid calcium influx and parasite immobilization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for fascioliasis, not clonorchiasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metronidazole treats amebiasis, not fluke infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paromomycin is a luminal amebicide, not an antihelminthic for flukes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Echinocandins treat fungal abscesses, not fluke infections.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old shepherd from a sheep-raising region has an incidentally found large hepatic cyst. CT shows a well-defined cyst with peripheral eggshell (curvilinear) calcification and internal daughter cysts. Which management approach is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Eggshell calcification with daughter cysts in a shepherd indicates a hydatid (Echinococcus) cyst, treated with albendazole and careful cyst management.
explanation.whyCorrect: Echinococcus granulosus hydatid disease presents as a calcified cyst with daughter cysts in sheep-associated exposures; albendazole is the antiparasitic backbone, with cyst management (e.g., PAIR or surgery) to avoid anaphylaxis from spillage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Metronidazole/paromomycin treats amebic abscess, not a calcified hydatid cyst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Praziquantel is used for flukes and adjunctively in some echinococcosis, but it is not the primary agent and is inadequate as monotherapy here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotics and simple drainage are for pyogenic abscess; uncontrolled aspiration of a hydatid cyst risks anaphylaxis and dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Triclabendazole treats fascioliasis, not echinococcal cysts.

questions.stem: A physician contrasts amebic and pyogenic liver abscesses. Which statement most accurately distinguishes them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amebic abscesses are usually multiloculated; pyogenic abscesses are solitary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amebic abscesses almost always require surgical drainage; pyogenic rarely do

choices.label: C
choices.text: Amebic abscesses preferentially involve the left lobe; pyogenic the right

choices.label: D
choices.text: Amebic abscesses grow gram-negative rods on culture; pyogenic are sterile

choices.label: E
choices.text: Amebic abscesses are usually solitary; pyogenic abscesses are often multiple

explanation.summary: Amebic abscesses are typically solitary, whereas pyogenic abscesses are often multiple.
explanation.whyCorrect: A key distinguishing feature is that amebic abscesses are usually single/solitary while pyogenic abscesses are frequently multiple and multiloculated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the pattern; amebic abscesses are solitary and pyogenic are often multiloculated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Most amebic abscesses respond to metronidazole without drainage, while pyogenic abscesses commonly require drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amebic abscesses favor the right lobe due to portal streaming, not the left.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amebic aspirate is typically sterile of bacteria (anchovy paste); pyogenic abscesses yield bacterial cultures.

questions.stem: A hospital protocol committee is selecting the gold-standard imaging modality for confirming and characterizing hepatic abscess, particularly before liquefaction is complete. Which modality should be designated?

explanation.summary: CT is the gold-standard imaging modality for hepatic abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT provides excellent visualization and characterization of hepatic abscesses and is the gold standard, whereas ultrasound may be suboptimal if the abscess has not yet liquefied.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ultrasound is often the first test but is less sensitive before liquefaction and is not the gold standard.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plain radiographs lack the resolution to characterize hepatic abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIDA scans assess biliary excretion/cystic duct patency, not abscess characterization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ERCP is a biliary intervention, not a primary imaging modality for parenchymal abscess.

questions.stem: A patient with fascioliasis is treated with triclabendazole. Approximately 7 to 10 days later he develops right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. Which complication of therapy best explains this?

explanation.summary: Triclabendazole can precipitate biliary obstruction 7 to 10 days after treatment as dead flukes lodge in the ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: After triclabendazole kills the flukes, dead worms and debris can obstruct the biliary tree roughly 7 to 10 days later, causing RUQ pain and jaundice.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immune hemolytic anemia is not the characteristic delayed complication of triclabendazole in fascioliasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pancreatitis is not the classically described post-triclabendazole event in this timeframe.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anaphylaxis from hydatid cyst rupture relates to echinococcal disease, not triclabendazole therapy for Fasciola.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serotonin syndrome is unrelated to antihelminthic therapy for liver flukes.

questions.stem: An emergency physician is about to start empiric therapy for a patient with a presumed pyogenic liver abscess of biliary origin before culture results return. Which empiric coverage is most appropriate?

choices.label: C
choices.text: An agent active only against intestinal anaerobes

explanation.summary: Pyogenic abscesses are often polymicrobial, so empiric therapy must be broad.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because pyogenic liver abscesses of biliary/GI origin are frequently polymicrobial, empiric IV therapy must cover gram-negative rods, anaerobes, and gram-positive cocci until cultures guide narrowing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vancomycin monotherapy misses gram-negative rods and anaerobes central to biliary-source abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anaerobe-only coverage omits the gram-negative rods (e.g., E coli) that predominate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metronidazole plus paromomycin targets amebiasis, not a polymicrobial bacterial abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fluconazole targets fungi, which are not the cause of a typical biliary-source pyogenic abscess.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man from Southeast Asia who ate raw freshwater fish decades ago presents now with cholangitis. He is told the responsible flukes can persist in his biliary tree for an extended period. Approximately how long can liver flukes remain dormant in the intrahepatic bile ducts?

explanation.summary: Liver flukes can remain dormant in the intrahepatic bile ducts for up to about 30 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liver flukes can persist and remain dormant in the intrahepatic bile ducts for up to roughly 30 years, explaining late presentations decades after exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Six months greatly underestimates fluke persistence in the biliary tree.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two years underestimates the up-to-30-year dormancy period.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ten years is still short of the documented persistence of up to about 30 years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sixty years exceeds the commonly cited up-to-30-year duration.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C, detectable HCV RNA, mildly elevated transaminases, and no evidence of cirrhosis on ultrasound asks whether the virus can be cured. She is otherwise well and takes no medications. Which class of agents offers her the highest likelihood of viral eradication?

explanation.summary: Modern oral DAA regimens cure chronic HCV in more than 95 percent of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Direct-acting antivirals targeting NS3/4A, NS5B, and NS5A are the standard of care for chronic HCV, achieving sustained virologic response (cure) rates greater than 95 percent with well-tolerated oral therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon-based therapy is now reserved as a last resort because it has lower efficacy and far more adverse effects than DAAs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Entecavir and other nucleos(t)ide analogs treat hepatitis B, not hepatitis C.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribavirin alone does not cure HCV and carries a risk of hemolytic anemia and teratogenicity; it is only an adjunct in select DAA regimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Older interferon-plus-ribavirin regimens have been supplanted by DAAs, which offer higher cure rates without injection-related toxicity.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is started on a hepatitis C medication whose generic name ends in the suffix -buvir. His clinician explains it is incorporated into the growing viral RNA strand and causes chain termination. Which viral protein does this drug inhibit?

explanation.summary: The -buvir suffix identifies NS5B polymerase inhibitors such as sofosbuvir.
explanation.whyCorrect: Agents ending in -buvir (e.g., sofosbuvir, dasabuvir) inhibit the NS5B RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; nucleotide analog -buvirs are incorporated into nascent HCV RNA and cause chain termination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NS3/4A protease inhibitors carry the -previr suffix and block post-translational cleavage of the viral polyprotein, not RNA chain elongation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NS5A inhibitors carry the -svir suffix and impair replication complex assembly, not polymerase-mediated chain elongation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HBV DNA polymerase is the target of anti-HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs, not HCV -buvir drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No approved DAA class works by blocking a viral entry receptor.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with chronic HCV begins a regimen that includes ribavirin. Two weeks later she reports fatigue and pallor, and her hemoglobin has dropped from 13.5 to 9.8 g/dL with an elevated reticulocyte count and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Which adverse effect of ribavirin explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aplastic anemia from bone marrow suppression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia from gastrointestinal blood loss

explanation.summary: Ribavirin's most important toxicity is dose-dependent hemolytic anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ribavirin accumulates in erythrocytes and causes an early, dose-dependent hemolytic anemia, reflected by a falling hemoglobin, elevated reticulocytes, and indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The elevated reticulocyte count indicates a compensating, active marrow, arguing against aplastic anemia; ribavirin causes hemolysis rather than marrow aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no evidence of GI bleeding, and hemolysis (not iron loss) is indicated by the reticulocytosis and indirect hyperbilirubinemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Megaloblastic anemia produces a low reticulocyte count and macrocytosis, not the hemolytic picture seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anemia of chronic disease develops gradually with a low reticulocyte response, unlike this rapid hemolytic drop.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with both chronic hepatitis B (HBV) and chronic hepatitis C (HCV) is being evaluated. Why can a single nucleotide analog such as tenofovir be effective against HBV even though it was developed as an antiretroviral for HIV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HBV and HIV share identical envelope glycoproteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: HBV uses the same NS5B polymerase as HCV

choices.label: D
choices.text: HBV DNA polymerase possesses reverse transcriptase activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: HBV replicates exclusively as a positive-sense RNA virus

explanation.summary: HBV DNA polymerase has reverse transcriptase activity, so RT-inhibiting nucleos(t)ide analogs work against both HBV and HIV.
explanation.whyCorrect: HBV replicates its DNA genome through a reverse-transcription step, and its polymerase has reverse transcriptase activity. Tenofovir diphosphate inhibits this RT step, giving it activity against both HBV and HIV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Shared envelope glycoproteins are not why tenofovir works; the drug acts intracellularly on the polymerase, not the envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tenofovir is a chain-terminating nucleotide analog, not an immune stimulant like interferon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NS5B is an HCV protein; HBV does not use it, and tenofovir does not target NS5B.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HBV is a partially double-stranded DNA virus that uses reverse transcription, not a positive-sense RNA virus.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic HBV is started on tenofovir. After intracellular activation, the drug is incorporated into the growing viral DNA strand. Which structural feature of the incorporated nucleotide analog produces obligate chain termination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An additional phosphate at the 5' position

choices.label: C
choices.text: A halogen substitution on the sugar

explanation.summary: Chain-terminating nucleos(t)ide analogs lack a 3'-OH, preventing the next phosphodiester bond.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tenofovir diphosphate competes with dATP and is incorporated into viral DNA, but because it lacks a 3'-hydroxyl group the polymerase cannot add the next nucleotide, causing obligate chain termination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An extra 5' phosphate does not block elongation; chain extension depends on the availability of the 3'-OH acceptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Base methylation does not prevent phosphodiester bond formation and is not the mechanism of chain termination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A sugar halogen substitution is not what terminates the chain; the missing 3'-OH is the critical feature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phosphonate group relates to tenofovir's resistance to hydrolysis, not to chain termination, which is caused by the absent 3'-OH.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with chronic HBV that is resistant to lamivudine needs an alternative oral agent. Her clinician selects a guanosine nucleoside analog that competes with dGTP and inhibits base priming, reverse transcription of the pregenomic RNA, and positive-strand HBV DNA synthesis. Which drug was chosen?

explanation.summary: Entecavir is a guanosine analog effective against lamivudine-resistant HBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Entecavir triphosphate competes with dGTP and inhibits HBV base priming, reverse transcription of pregenomic RNA, and positive-strand DNA synthesis; it retains activity against lamivudine-resistant strains.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sofosbuvir is an HCV NS5B polymerase inhibitor and has no role in treating HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ledipasvir is an HCV NS5A inhibitor, not an anti-HBV agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribavirin is a guanosine analog used as an adjunct in HCV, not a treatment for HBV, and does not overcome lamivudine resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Grazoprevir is an HCV NS3/4A protease inhibitor and is inactive against HBV.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with chronic HCV is trying to conceive. Her physician emphasizes that one component sometimes added to HCV regimens is absolutely contraindicated in her situation and requires two forms of contraception in both partners. Which agent is being described?

explanation.summary: Ribavirin is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ribavirin is a known teratogen; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and requires two reliable forms of contraception in both the patient and her partner during and after treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sofosbuvir is not a recognized teratogen and is not the agent requiring dual contraception in both partners.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ledipasvir, an NS5A inhibitor, does not carry ribavirin's specific teratogenicity warning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Entecavir treats HBV and is not the HCV adjunct described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Glecaprevir, an NS3/4A protease inhibitor, is not the teratogen requiring two forms of contraception in both partners.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with genotype 1 chronic HCV starts a regimen containing an NS3/4A protease inhibitor. His pharmacist flags several potential drug interactions with his other medications. Inhibition of which system best explains these interactions?

explanation.summary: NS3/4A protease inhibitors inhibit CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, producing many drug interactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The -previr protease inhibitors inhibit CYP3A4 and the P-glycoprotein transporter, so they raise levels of many co-administered drugs and are a major source of interactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The RAAS is unrelated to protease inhibitor drug interactions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Xanthine oxidase inhibition (e.g., allopurinol) is not a property of -previr agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monoamine oxidase inhibition is not the mechanism behind protease inhibitor interactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: COX-2 inhibition is a feature of certain NSAIDs, not HCV protease inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 41-year-old man begins therapy for chronic HCV. He starts a medication whose generic name ends in -svir (not a -previr). This drug does not have enzymatic catalytic activity but is essential for assembly of the viral replication complex. Which viral protein does it target?

explanation.summary: NS5A inhibitors (-svir, e.g., ledipasvir, daclatasvir) target the non-enzymatic NS5A protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: NS5A is a non-enzymatic phosphoprotein required for HCV RNA replication and virion assembly. Inhibitors such as ledipasvir and daclatasvir (-svir suffix) block these functions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NS3/4A is an enzyme (serine protease) targeted by -previr drugs, not -svir agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NS5B is the enzymatic RNA polymerase targeted by -buvir drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HBV reverse transcriptase is targeted by anti-HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs, not HCV NS5A inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P-glycoprotein is a host transporter, not the viral target of NS5A inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with HBV/HCV co-infection has a contraindication to first-line oral regimens and is treated with an older injectable immune-based agent that activates antiviral genes and stimulates cell-mediated immunity against both viruses. This drug is now reserved as a last resort. Which agent was used?

explanation.summary: Interferon alpha-2a has activity against both HBV and HCV and is reserved as a last resort.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interferon alpha-2a activates interferon-responsive antiviral genes and stimulates cell-mediated immunity. It has activity against both HBV and HCV but, because of poor tolerability and lower efficacy than DAAs, it is now a last-resort agent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sofosbuvir treats HCV only and works by inhibiting NS5B, not by immune stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tenofovir treats HBV (and HIV) but not HCV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Entecavir treats HBV only and is not an immune-based agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glecaprevir is an HCV-specific NS3/4A protease inhibitor without activity against HBV.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic HBV begins entecavir. One week later he develops new bilateral 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities without dyspnea, and his cardiac and renal workup is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A recognized adverse effect of entecavir

explanation.summary: Peripheral edema is a recognized adverse effect of entecavir, occurring in roughly 16 percent of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Edema occurs in about 16 percent of patients treated with entecavir and, in the absence of cardiac or renal disease, is best attributed to the drug itself.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The patient has HBV and is on entecavir, not ribavirin; ribavirin causes hemolytic anemia, not isolated edema.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The patient is not receiving interferon, and edema here is a direct entecavir effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sofosbuvir is an HCV agent not being used, and heart failure was excluded by an unremarkable cardiac workup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ledipasvir is an HCV drug not prescribed here, and no proteinuria/nephrotic findings are described.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with chronic HCV is started on a regimen containing sofosbuvir. Her clinician reviews her medication list to avoid an agent that could lower sofosbuvir concentrations and cause treatment failure. Co-administration of which type of drug is the primary concern?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A proton pump inhibitor that raises gastric pH

explanation.summary: Sofosbuvir is a P-glycoprotein substrate, so P-gp inducers can reduce its levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sofosbuvir is a substrate of P-glycoprotein. Potent P-gp inducers (e.g., rifampin, St. John's wort) lower sofosbuvir concentrations and can lead to loss of efficacy, so they should not be co-administered.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CYP3A4 inhibitor would tend to raise, not lower, substrate levels, and sofosbuvir's key interaction is via P-gp, not CYP3A4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loop diuretics do not meaningfully alter sofosbuvir pharmacokinetics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric pH changes from PPIs are a concern for some NS5A combination pills (e.g., ledipasvir absorption), not the P-gp-mediated sofosbuvir interaction described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-blockers do not induce P-glycoprotein or reduce sofosbuvir exposure.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic HBV asks how long he must take his nucleoside analog. He expects a short course like an antibiotic. Which statement most accurately describes the expected duration of nucleos(t)ide analog therapy for chronic HBV?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A minimum of about 4 years and potentially indefinite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exactly 12 weeks, matching HCV DAA courses

explanation.summary: Nucleos(t)ide analog therapy for chronic HBV lasts a minimum of about 4 years and may be indefinite.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because HBV is suppressed but not cured, nucleos(t)ide analog therapy is long-term, lasting a minimum of roughly 4 years and often continued indefinitely depending on serologic and virologic response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A brief loading course does not control chronic HBV, which requires sustained suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A two-week course is far too short; HBV rebounds when suppression stops prematurely.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 12-week fixed course applies to many HCV DAA regimens, not to long-term HBV suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intermittent treatment only during flares does not adequately suppress ongoing HBV replication.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 44-year-old man receiving interferon alpha-2a for chronic viral hepatitis reports diffuse muscle aches, joint pains, insomnia, and low mood, and his labs show a mild neutropenia. Approximately what fraction of patients experience this cluster of interferon-related adverse effects?

explanation.summary: Roughly 19 to 28 percent of interferon alpha-2a patients develop myalgias, arthralgia, insomnia, irritability, neutropenia, and transaminitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interferon alpha-2a commonly causes a flu-like and neuropsychiatric adverse effect profile, with approximately 19 to 28 percent of patients experiencing myalgias, arthralgia, insomnia, irritability, neutropenia, and transaminitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These effects are common, not rare; well under 1 percent grossly underestimates their frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 2 to 4 percent rate underestimates the frequency of interferon's flu-like and mood symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An 8 to 10 percent estimate is still lower than the reported 19 to 28 percent range.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Greater than 80 percent overestimates the incidence of this specific symptom cluster.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A physician wants to prescribe interferon for a patient with chronic hepatitis but improve dosing convenience compared with standard interferon alpha-2a, which requires frequent injections. Which formulation allows once-weekly subcutaneous dosing, and what modification enables this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Liposomal interferon; encapsulation in lipid vesicles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pegylated interferon alpha-2a; attachment of polyethylene glycol

explanation.summary: Pegylation extends interferon's half-life, permitting once-weekly dosing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Covalent attachment of a polyethylene glycol (PEG) molecule slows clearance and prolongs the half-life of interferon alpha-2a, allowing convenient once-weekly subcutaneous administration; this is why pegylated interferon is preferred over the standard form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Liposomal encapsulation is not the modification used; PEG conjugation is what extends interferon's dosing interval.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Interferon is a protein degraded in the gut and is not given orally; enteric coating does not enable weekly dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recombinant bacterial expression describes how interferon is manufactured, not what prolongs its half-life.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Consensus interferon (interferon alfacon-1) is a distinct engineered molecule, but weekly dosing here is achieved through pegylation, not amino acid substitution.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A medical student is asked why hepatitis B is described as controllable but not yet curable with current drugs, whereas hepatitis C is considered curable. Which statement best captures the correct comparison?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HBV nucleos(t)ide analogs suppress replication but do not eradicate the virus, whereas HCV DAAs achieve cure in over 95 percent of patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: HBV is cured in a single 12-week course while HCV requires lifelong therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both HBV and HCV are cured by the same nucleoside analogs

choices.label: D
choices.text: HCV cannot be cured, but HBV is routinely eradicated with entecavir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither infection can be treated with available antiviral drugs

explanation.summary: HBV therapy suppresses but does not cure; HCV DAAs cure over 95 percent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nucleos(t)ide analogs for HBV durably suppress viral replication but do not eliminate covalently closed circular DNA, so HBV is controlled rather than cured. In contrast, modern HCV DAA regimens achieve sustained virologic response (cure) in more than 95 percent of patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the truth: HCV is the one cured by short courses; HBV often requires long-term or indefinite therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HBV and HCV are treated with distinct drug classes because antivirals have a narrow spectrum; they are not cured by the same agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HCV is curable, and entecavir suppresses but does not eradicate HBV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both infections are treatable with effective antiviral drugs; this statement is simply false.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: Before initiating direct-acting antiviral therapy in a patient with chronic HCV and a history of injection drug use, the clinician orders HIV testing. What is the primary reason HIV testing is recommended prior to HCV treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DAAs are ineffective in anyone who has ever injected drugs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Co-infection is common and alters drug choice because of interactions and regimen considerations

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV testing is required to diagnose HCV itself

choices.label: D
choices.text: DAAs cure HIV, so testing documents baseline status

choices.label: E
choices.text: HCV therapy is contraindicated if any prior IV drug use is reported

explanation.summary: HBV, HCV, and HIV share risk factors; co-infection changes DAA selection due to drug interactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because HBV, HCV, and HIV share transmission routes, co-infection is common. Identifying HIV co-infection matters because it alters DAA regimen choice and raises the risk of clinically important drug-drug interactions with antiretroviral therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A history of injection drug use does not make DAAs ineffective; cure rates remain high.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HCV is diagnosed by HCV RNA and antibody testing, not by an HIV test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DAAs do not cure HIV; they target HCV proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prior IV drug use is not a contraindication to HCV therapy; such patients are strong candidates for cure.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A hepatologist maps four antiviral drugs to their targets in the viral life cycle: entecavir, sofosbuvir, glecaprevir, and daclatasvir. Which drug-to-target pairing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Entecavir inhibits the HCV NS5B polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daclatasvir inhibits the HCV NS3/4A protease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glecaprevir inhibits the HCV NS3/4A protease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sofosbuvir inhibits the HCV NS5A protein

explanation.summary: Glecaprevir is a -previr NS3/4A protease inhibitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glecaprevir carries the -previr suffix and inhibits the HCV NS3/4A serine protease responsible for post-translational cleavage of the viral polyprotein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Entecavir inhibits HBV DNA polymerase, not the HCV NS5B polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Daclatasvir is an NS5A inhibitor (-svir), not an NS3/4A protease inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sofosbuvir inhibits the NS5B polymerase (-buvir), not NS5A.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Daclatasvir targets HCV NS5A, not HBV DNA polymerase.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and moderate renal impairment has chronic HCV. Her team wants to minimize adverse effects and specifically avoids an adjunctive agent that can worsen anemia, is teratogenic, and is relatively contraindicated in significant pulmonary and renal disease. Which agent are they avoiding?

explanation.summary: Ribavirin causes hemolytic anemia and is problematic in COPD, renal disease, and pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ribavirin causes dose-dependent hemolytic anemia, is teratogenic, and is relatively contraindicated in severe pulmonary disease (bronchoconstriction risk) and significant renal impairment (reduced clearance). Avoiding it minimizes harm in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sofosbuvir is generally well tolerated and does not carry ribavirin's hemolytic and pulmonary cautions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ledipasvir is a well-tolerated NS5A inhibitor without these specific contraindications.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Grazoprevir is an NS3/4A protease inhibitor and is not the agent defined by hemolysis plus pulmonary and renal cautions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tenofovir is an anti-HBV/HIV nucleotide analog, not an HCV adjunct with these particular contraindications.

questions.topicName: Drugs to Treat Hepatitis B and C Infections
questions.stem: A clinician counsels a patient starting HCV therapy that the overarching goals are viral eradication and prevention of long-term complications. Which pair of complications is the therapy specifically intended to prevent?

explanation.summary: The goals of HCV therapy are viral eradication and prevention of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sustained clearance of HCV halts ongoing hepatic injury, sharply reducing progression to cirrhosis and the subsequent risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, which are the principal complications the therapy aims to prevent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peptic ulcer disease and gastritis are not chronic HCV sequelae targeted by antiviral therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pancreatitis and cholelithiasis are not the liver-specific complications HCV treatment aims to prevent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diverticulitis and colorectal cancer are unrelated to chronic hepatitis C progression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal stones and glomerulonephritis are not the primary hepatic outcomes addressed by HCV cure.

questions.topicName: Noninfectious Disorders of the Biliary System
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with episodes of dull, cramping right upper quadrant pain that begin about 30 minutes after eating a fatty meal, radiate to the right shoulder, and resolve on their own within about 2 hours. She is afebrile, her abdomen is soft and nontender, and her white blood cell count, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases are all normal. Ultrasound shows gallstones without wall thickening. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Self-limited postprandial RUQ pain with normal labs and no fever indicates biliary colic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Biliary colic occurs when a gallstone transiently obstructs the cystic duct, often after a fatty meal releases CCK; pain lasts less than 6 hours and the patient is stable, afebrile, with normal labs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute cholecystitis causes pain lasting more than 6 hours, fever, leukocytosis, and a positive Murphy sign from a persistently obstructed cystic duct.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ascending cholangitis produces the Charcot triad of fever, jaundice, and RUQ pain with an obstructed and infected bile duct, not normal labs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Choledocholithiasis would raise alkaline phosphatase and conjugated bilirubin from common bile duct obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gallstone pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated lipase, not brief self-limited colic.

questions.topicName: Noninfectious Disorders of the Biliary System
questions.stem: A 42-year-old obese woman with three children and a family history of gallstones is found to have cholesterol gallstones. Which of the following best describes the composition and predisposing factor of the most common type of gallstone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stones rich in bilirubin, associated with chronic hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stones formed from bile supersaturated with cholesterol, associated with obesity and female sex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stones composed of calcium carbonate, associated with hyperparathyroidism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stones formed from bacterial deconjugation of bilirubin, associated with biliary infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stones composed primarily of bile salts, associated with ileal resection

explanation.summary: Cholesterol stones are the most common (about 80%) and form from cholesterol-supersaturated bile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cholesterol gallstones account for roughly 80% of stones and form when bile is supersaturated with cholesterol; classic risk factors are the six Fs: Female, Fertile, Fat, Forty, Family, and Farmacology (octreotide, ceftriaxone).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bilirubin-rich stones associated with hemolysis are pigment stones, which make up only about 20%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium carbonate composition is not the described most common stone type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacterial deconjugation produces brown pigment stones in the setting of biliary infection, not the majority cholesterol stones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ileal resection depletes the bile acid pool and predisposes to cholesterol stones, but the stones are cholesterol, not bile salts.

questions.topicName: Noninfectious Disorders of the Biliary System
